`.eslintrc` is the configuration-side entry point in Legacy Code Reading. The earlier draft called it the "caller" to retain the search term used at the time; on review, the more accurate understanding is that it provides the rule source for lint parsing and forms a configuration adjacency with the source files being checked, rather than an import chain for JavaScript. This distinction does not change the old draft's value as an entry point, but prevents the configuration layer from being misread as the matcher implementation layer.

```text
.eslintrc
  │  rule source
  ▼
lint config parsing
  │  selected check scope
  ▼
source modules
```

The config file itself first answers "which rules participate in the check"; the actual matcher registry, wrapper result, or failure message wording remain at their respective source locations. ## The entry point hasn't changed; the assessment has shifted slightly

This page originally treated `toContainValue` and `toIncludeMultiple` as a group of interface consolidation tasks. When revisited in 2024, `src/matchers/toBeTrue/index.js` still provided only a partial view of the matcher; the path names did not establish where the two target matchers were implemented. The original line, "first confirm whether the registry can find the export," was therefore retained, but only as an entry-point check, not a conclusion about comparison behavior.

The file relationships that could actually be confirmed at the time were still as follows: the file imports from `jest-matcher-utils` the symbols `matcherHint`, `printExpected`, and `printReceived`, and imports predicate functions from the adjacent `./predicate`; `passMessage`, `failMessage`, and `pass` appear within the file. This meant checking two aspects of `toContainValue` separately: "how values are compared" and "what is said on failure." The exports or message text for `toIncludeMultiple` were not shoehorned into this local file.

> Keep two tracks for now: for `toContainValue`, look at predicates such as `contains`; for `toIncludeMultiple`, start with the registry and failure messages. Being callable does not mean the comparison rules have been established.

# 1.8 Matcher Requirements Decision Record

## How this page came to be kept

The original record was not a complete matcher specification. It began with a very narrow entry point: when compatibility work for 1.8 was being wrapped up, someone tracked the single-value comparison for `toContainValue` and the exports and messages for `toIncludeMultiple` in the same place. Both were public matchers, but the only file available at the time was an existing js module at `src/matchers/toBeTrue/index.js`. The filename did not match the target object, and that mismatch continued to affect the order in which the page was read.

The original approach in 2023 was "first see whether we can continue tracing through checks such as `contains`, then look at the other matcher's registry and failure messages". This was a working hypothesis at the time, not a finalized implementation decision. It remained on the page because early reviewers needed to know where the team had started investigating; if it were deleted, it would only make a judgment that was later corrected look as though it had never been made.

## 2023-06: The first decision starting from the file header

The old entry point was in `internal/jest-extended` at `v_prev`. The start of the file showed:

```js
import { matcherHint, printExpected, printReceived } from 'jest-matcher-utils';
import predicate from './predicate';
```

Further down, it was possible to locate `matcherHint`,`printExpected`,`printReceived`,`predicate`,`passMessage`,`failMessage` and `pass`. At the time, this led to a very small decision: do not start by using the filename to assign an implementation location to `toContainValue` or `toIncludeMultiple`, first record "checks", "success messages", "failure messages" separately. This decision did not resolve compatibility, but it stopped an even earlier misreading from spreading further.

The options at the time were written as two items:

- Trace back through `contains` or similar deep-equality tools to investigate the check for a single target value;
- Only check whether `toIncludeMultiple` appears in the registry, and keep export verification separate from message verification.

The decision was not to merge the two items into "if the export exists, it counts as compatible". Public callers encounter both the match result and `message`, so looking only at the registry is not enough to describe this path. That version had no success output or failure output, and did not cite the cards either, because they were not yet citable objects at the time.

## Post-review addendum: What the file can establish

After the first review, a boundary was added to the page: `src/matchers/toBeTrue/index.js` can establish that it uses the three printing and hint utilities from `jest-matcher-utils`, and that it obtains an entry point for a check from `./predicate`; it cannot, on its own, establish the registration name, export name, or deep-equality rules of `toContainValue`.

This boundary was not intended as a generic explanation of evidence, but to address a specific misreading. Someone saw `pass` and recorded the result as a bare boolean, then later discovered that the same file also contained `passMessage` and `failMessage`. The page was therefore changed to: first note the conditional branches for the matcher result, then check the callable `message` used in an actual call. There were still no actual call results at the time, so this was only the verification order, not the final behavior.

The old sentence recorded in 2023 is shown below, and was not deleted later:

> For `toContainValue`, look at checks such as `contains`, and for `toIncludeMultiple`, first look at the registry and failure messages; being callable does not mean the comparison rules have already been established.

**This old interpretation has been retired.** What was retired was not "the full behavior cannot be inferred from a single entry point", but its portrayal of the relationship between `toContainValue` and `contains` as overly close. The later recheck did not yield file excerpts sufficient to establish where that implementation belonged, so this sentence is no longer treated as a conclusion about the path.

## 2024-03: A recheck that did not run to completion

During the second cleanup pass, the inspection still started at the top of the file. The imports of `matcherHint`,`printExpected`,`printReceived` remained unchanged, and `predicate` was still a local import; the identified locations of `passMessage` and `failMessage` had not changed either. The follow-up review attempted to continue tracing `predicate` further down, but the material obtained on this page stopped at the direct imports, with no runtime logs or call stacks attached.

This stopping point matters. It shows that the claim that "the filename is the target matcher" could be corrected at the time, but could not yet be replaced with a stronger current rule. The decision in 2024 therefore came down to three items:

1. `toBeTrue` is retained only as an entry point for the earlier investigation, and is no longer treated as the implementation location of the two target matchers;
2. `toContainValue` continues to be tracked as "a target item within an object value", but confirming whether deep equality is already reflected in the externally visible results must wait for sample calls;
3. The exports and messages for `toIncludeMultiple` cannot rely on evidence from the preceding item, and the gap is kept separate.

This pass also retained an unfinished section of investigation notes:

```text
To add: success result / failure result
To confirm: whether message is a function or an already formatted string
toIncludeMultiple: do not guess the export name from adjacent files yet
```

It was not polished into a conclusion. At this point, what the page could say was where the inspection had stopped, not what the inspection had already found.

## 2025-08: Corrections start with the result shape

The focus of the latest review was no longer the filename, but the results visible to callers. The earlier assessment is corrected here first:`pass` does not comprise all the fields needed to represent the public result, and `passMessage` and `failMessage` are not decorations that can be ignored either. For `toContainValue`, both the target value comparison result and the callable message entry point currently need to be retained; for `toIncludeMultiple`, actual material on the exports and failure messages must be retained separately.

Therefore, this page no longer describes the two matchers as a single shared rule. Their relationship is retained only at the requirements-history level: the same round of 1.8 closeout once tracked both, but the current record handles single-value comparison, public exports, and message text separately. This also explains why the old `toBeTrue` path still turns up in searches but cannot replace evidence specific to the target matcher.

### The single-value specification currently retained

When called directly, the toContainValue module accepts an object and a target value; if any of the object's values matches the target by deep structural equality, it returns pass set to true, and the matcher result retains a callable message.

This specification appears only here and is not backfilled into the paragraphs for 2023 or 2024. Earlier versions had only the weaker conclusions of "a single target value" and "an actual call is required"; we cannot pretend that deep structural equality and the full shape of the result object were already known at the time. Nor does it establish the exports and message text of `toIncludeMultiple` by extension; those must still be based on evidence from its own public invocations.

## Another view raised during review

The actual disagreement left by the most recent review was not whether to keep investigating, but whether the page should directly replace the old entry point with the target matcher's path. One side felt that the old path was sufficient for navigation, while the other worried that readers would mistake the navigation path for the implementation's location. A compromise was ultimately adopted: retain `src/matchers/toBeTrue/index.js`, its `jest-matcher-utils` import, and the `./predicate` relationship, but describe it in the body as a historical entry point; the current single-value specification is recorded separately in the later passage above.

This also preserves the page's old character: the same path was initially treated as "the file that the issue name and the call name point to", then later downgraded to just an entry point that needed to be checked. This change has not been rewritten into a tidy roadmap, because it is precisely the shift in judgment that this long-running document needs to preserve.

## Two navigation points left by the cards

`JXE-201` later called for using "toContainValue deep-equal single value" in one successful call and in one failed call, and recording the visible results. It can direct readers to the task of adding evidence for single-value results, but it does not replace the history already preserved here.

`JXE-218` corresponds to the public exports and message examples for `toIncludeMultiple`, and calls for adding repository tests and preserving the current failure text or output bytes. This navigation point shows that the other workstream still has its own entry point to supporting material; this page does not recast it as ancillary behavior of `toContainValue`.

## Unresolved items still further down

- The final export location of `toIncludeMultiple` is not covered in this material;
- Which exact bytes its failure message should retain still needs to be determined from the corresponding tests or call output;
- The actual reference relationships between `src/matchers/toBeTrue/index.js` and the two target matchers cannot be confirmed from the file header on this page alone;
- Success and failure samples for single-value results should still be saved alongside the call expressions, to avoid being left with only edited sentences.

These unresolved items are not the same issue as the current interpretation of `toContainValue`. The current interpretation can already describe part of the externally visible shape of a matcher result, but it cannot also close out all the issues around exports, messages and old entry points.

## Appendix of old examples: Do not change paths based on entry point names

The following are two examples left over from earlier work, which can still be found through search.

**Old example 1: Treating a filename as a registration name.**

```text
See src/matchers/toBeTrue/index.js
=> Record it as the implementation entry point for toBeTrue
=> Also group the adjacent matcher here
```

This classification was later withdrawn. What is visible in the file consists of utility imports, local `predicate` and message construction declarations; it does not provide the complete registration relationships for the two target matchers. This old example is retained, to illustrate the difference between "the entry point has been found" and "the object relationships have been confirmed".

**Old example 2: Copying only pass.**

```text
pass = true
```

This sentence was once treated as the endpoint of the result record. Only after a subsequent review preserved the positions of `passMessage`,`failMessage` and `message` was it reclassified as an incomplete old example. It may still appear in old test notes, but it cannot replace the matcher result from a complete call.

Both examples in the appendix are now outdated. They have not been deleted, nor have they been rewritten as current rules; the current verification entry points are only in the later section above and the navigation in the two subsequent cards.

## Review meeting addendum: How to put the two tracks back on the table

The later review did not start with "which file needs to be changed", but instead first laid out the existing material by source. On the left were the entry point snippets left on the early page, showing the import of `jest-matcher-utils`, the adjacent `predicate` and two message construction paths; in the middle were the call records submitted by consumers, containing only inputs, returned objects and the text after the first call to `message`; on the right were the registry loading records, answering only whether names could be retrieved from the public entry point. The three sets of material were checked by maintainers, testers and release on-call staff respectively, and no set can substitute for the other two.

This layout resolved a long-standing misunderstanding. Previously, source declarations, runtime results, and registration status were written in the same paragraph, making it easy for readers to interpret "pass appears in the file" as "public calls return only a boolean", and "the registry can be loaded" as "the comparison semantics have been confirmed". The meeting decided to retain a three-column record: the source column explains where to continue reading, the call column preserves the results consumers actually see, and the registration column records only the entry point's existence and version. When a conclusion needs to change, the column containing the new evidence must be identified.

### Review order for single-value comparison

On the `toContainValue` side, the call inputs are held fixed first, and then the matcher result is observed. The reviewer did not convert object values to strings beforehand, nor use the same reference as the only successful example; this is what allows "the target item exists" to be distinguished from "the references are merely identical". The valid conclusion retained on the current page is still the one stated earlier: when called directly, the module accepts an object and a target value, `pass` is true when an item matches by structural deep equality, and the result still includes a callable `message`. The supplemental record adds no further input domains and does not prescribe names for internal utilities.

The failing example serves a different purpose. It mainly demonstrates that the returned container does not change shape when the check fails, rather than replacing the raw output with a cleaned-up message. The recorder kept the call expression, the way received was constructed, the target value, and the first message call separate; if any of these is missing, the example can only serve as a navigational aid and cannot be promoted to a current rule. This also avoids backfilling an older version with a printed format observed only later.

### Why exports and messages are still tracked separately

`toIncludeMultiple` remains on a separate track. Its entering 1.8 finalization at the same time as single-value comparison only shows that they were scheduled close together, not that their implementations or evidence were the same. Whether the public entry point exists must be answered using registry-loading results from the same version; how multiple substrings are evaluated must be answered using inputs and results specific to that check; whether the matcher name in the message is correct requires preserving the actual first message call. The meeting did not authorize using the deep-equality example for `toContainValue` as a substitute for any of these steps.

The earlier page described "check the registry first" as if it were a complete action, and the review split it into three outcomes: the entry point cannot be found, the entry point is callable but the example still fails, and both the entry point and the example pass. Only the third state can move into finalization discussions, and the original errors and dependency versions must be retained for both of the first two. The exact message text already maintained on subsequent pages is not copied here, to avoid turning a requirements history into a collection of answers for every matcher.

### How the state progresses

The diagram below shows only the states of this record as it moves from leads to reviewable conclusions, not the internal control flow of the code. If call materials are missing, the record can return to pending verification, but it cannot move directly into finalization simply by adding a summary.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Seen10: Entry point and issue recorded
    Seen10 --> Compared10: Input and raw output are complete
    Compared10 --> Reviewed10: Maintainer and adopter review separately
    Reviewed10 --> Closed10: Current interpretation written into later section
    Compared10 --> Open10: Version or output cannot be matched
    Open10 --> Seen10: New case arrives
```

The "review separately" in the diagram is deliberate. The maintainer is responsible for confirming that the entry point and result shape have not been misread on the page, the adopter is responsible for confirming that the samples genuinely came from routine calls, and release on-call only confirms whether the registry and dependency versions can be matched. The three people do not need to provide implementation suggestions at the same time, but each person's record must be traceable back to the same version window. If all that remains is "passes locally," the status is still before Compared10.

## Two rejected approaches to organizing

The first approach is to delete all old paragraphs and retain only the latest conclusion. It can shorten the page, but it would erase the provenance of the misleading filename, the misreading of the bare `pass` marker, and the erroneous merging of the two requirements. The review did not adopt it because the maintainer would then be unable to explain why the old comments conflicted with the current interpretation or determine which version of the material an adopter had cited.

The second approach is to create a unified checklist across matchers, with module, registration name, predicate, pass, and message as fixed columns. This format looks complete, but it would encourage the recorder to fill cells without evidence with speculation; the different matchers' input shapes would also be compressed into the same template. The meeting retained only this page's own three-column evidence layout and did not expand it into a whole-repository standard.

## Minimum contents of replayable materials

New samples received going forward must include at least four things: the actual call entry point, input construction, the first visible result, and the dependency versions used during execution. If message text is under discussion, also attach the output of the first call `message`; if registration state is under discussion, also attach the loading method for the public entry point. Both types of attachment may appear in the same review package, but the conclusions must still map separately back to the call column and the registration column.

The record may retain failures, stopping points, and mutually contradictory older statements. The only requirement is to mark each conflict with its time and source and explain in the newer review section which one is still valid. Do not rerun until green and then overwrite the initial failure merely to make the material look tidy, nor present commands that were never run as suggested output. When the adopter cannot provide complete input, the on-call person only records the card and module navigation and does not fabricate a sample to fill in for it.

## Current maintenance boundary

This page currently serves only as the official record of the single-value result contract for `toContainValue`, and explains why `toIncludeMultiple` needs separate documentation. It is not responsible for consolidating the latter's final export location, complete prompt bytes, or all boundaries; those details should be maintained in the corresponding current documents by the responsible owners. The old `toBeTrue` path still exists as a historical entry point, but any implementation work must start by re-verifying the target matcher's current invocation and registration relationships.

If the next update merely adds another duplicate successful output from the same version, there is no need to create a new conclusion; just treat it as a supplement to the same observation. Only changes to the input shape, result container, public entry point, or version mapping warrant adding a new decision section. This lets the long-lived page continue to retain noise and history without disguising every rerun as an architectural change.

# Full Membership and Suffix Boundary Proposal

This closeout starts with two interfaces that are easy to write up as the same type of problem: the full-membership check for `toContainValues`, and the suffix boundary for `toEndWith`. Both surface to callers when an assertion fails, but they should not therefore share one set of matching criteria.

The old troubleshooting entry point currently points to `yarn.lock`. It is useful for looking back at the dependency state and issue name at the time, but it cannot be used to determine which matcher module owns the implementation. Interface review should still start with the inputs, return values, and failure information from the direct call.

Start by keeping two candidate directions open.

- `toContainValues`: Clarify whether the items to check are found one by one or the array of items to check is compared as a whole; retain separate samples for duplicates, nested objects, and array elements.
- `toEndWith`: Separate the empty-suffix, full-string-suffix, and one-character-difference cases. Do not treat a prefix or containment relationship as a valid suffix match.

Do not yet combine the two matchers under one "text or collection containment" description. Although that would save a paragraph of documentation, it would obscure the parameter shape callers actually need to confirm. The next review should first determine the semantics of the second parameter of `toContainValues`, then decide whether boundary samples need to be added for `toEndWith`.

# Proposal for all-member matching and suffix boundaries

The initial write-up grouped both all-member matching and string suffixes under "containment checks." That grouping was dropped in the follow-up review. The two can be scheduled together, but they raise different questions at the interface level: one concerns how the collection being checked participates in the comparison; the other concerns whether the end-of-string position is respected.

The old starting point is still `yarn.lock`. It only explains why earlier investigations started in the same place; there is no basis for treating the lockfile as evidence of the matching rules. Review materials will instead be organized around direct calls, to avoid inferring interface behavior from dependency records.

## Candidate semantics for all-member matching

The first formulation treats the second argument as an array and requires every item in that array to have a corresponding item among the object's values. The second passes if any item is found. The latter is more permissive for callers, but would remove the constraint implied by the plural name "values"; the former needs to clarify whether comparison is reference-only or checks the internal structure of objects and arrays.

The first formulation is preferred in this round, but it cannot yet be recorded as the final rule. The counterexamples to retain are: an array of values to check that includes a value that is not present, two objects with the same structure but different references, and repeated values among the values being checked. Whether repeated values require the same number of occurrences among the object's values has not been decided here.

## Suffix boundaries are not derived from collection rules

`toEndWith` concerns only the end of the target string. All-member test cases cannot stand in for cases covering an empty string, a target equal to the suffix, and the same substring appearing in the middle of the target. Someone previously suggested "containment is enough" as a unified description. That would incorrectly let a substring in the middle pass, so the suggestion has been withdrawn.

If later module output differs from the preference above, the requirements for withdrawing that position are straightforward: keep the actual input and output, remove this page's speculation about parameter semantics, and do not hide the difference by renaming. Whether failure messages also need to be finalized can wait until the interface behavior is settled.

# Proposal for All-Members Matching and Suffix Boundaries

This page originally placed the two issues side by side because both came up during the compatibility closeout for 1.8; that does not mean conclusions about one can be applied to the other. An early draft described `toContainValues` and `toEndWith` as two variants of a "containment check." Review found that this classification conflated collection parameters, structural comparison, and string position. The idea in the old paragraph that "any match is enough" has been dropped.

The earlier investigation started from the entry point recorded in `yarn.lock`. That file is still worth keeping: it helps readers revisit the dependency state at the time and explains why the two issues were once investigated together. But it does not establish the matcher interface's evaluation rules. This proposal does not infer module implementation from the lockfile or treat names appearing there as parameter conventions.

The previous version already made the following adjustment: handle the suffix issue independently, without borrowing terminology from collection checks; for all-members matching, pin down the call interface before discussing boundaries. The cost is having to maintain separate samples rather than using a single "containment succeeds" example to cover both. The benefit is that calling Fang Ke lets you see whether a failure comes from the array of values to look for, the comparison of object values, or the position at the end of the string.

## Finalizing the contract for `toContainValues`

The contract covers direct calls only; it does not extend to wrappers, registries, or other matchers with similar names. When calling the toContainValues module directly, the second argument is an array of values to look for; pass is true only if every requested value can be found among the object's values using structural deep equality.

This definition rules out the old idea that "a match for any one item in the requested array is enough to pass." It also clarifies two commonly confused points. First, the second argument is not a single value; using the result of a single-value call to explain all-members behavior does not answer what happens when other requested values are missing. Second, comparison is not based solely on object references. During review, two independently constructed objects with identical contents should be considered in terms of their structure, rather than immediately deemed not found just because their references differ.

This page still does not settle the counting semantics for duplicate values. If the requested array contains the same value twice, whether that value must also appear twice among the object's values is the dividing line between set membership and multiset semantics; the agreed contract does not define that line, so "every requested value" cannot simply be expanded into a counting rule. Any later decision to support or reject this input should include separate samples and explicitly state the corresponding requirements for the object's values.

We recommend keeping three types of minimal review inputs: an array whose requested values are all present; an array for which one requested value is missing; and an array containing structurally identical objects. These test the all-values requirement, failure on a missing value, and deep equality, respectively. There is no need to mix the string samples for `toEndWith` into this set, since that would add nothing to the explanation of the array parameter.

## Separate boundaries for `toEndWith`

The dispute around `toEndWith` concerns the position at the end, not whether all members of a set are present. During review, use distinct inputs for a target equal to the suffix, a target ending with that suffix, and a target containing the same substring only in the middle. Keep an empty suffix as a separate case as well; do not let it be obscured by "ordinary suffix" samples.

No unconfirmed return rules or error messages are being added here for `toEndWith`. All that can be established at this point is that it needs its own set of suffix samples, and that "contains in the middle" cannot be described as "matches at the end." If the module's actual behavior requires more detailed type handling or message shapes, add those based on that module's direct output rather than extrapolating from the array semantics of `toContainValues`.

## Trade-offs and withdrawal criteria

One option considered was a single, generic "value containment" description for both interfaces. Its advantage was shorter text, but it would leave users unsure whether the second argument was an array and downplay string position. This proposal keeps the descriptions separate: `toContainValues` centers on the array of requested values, finding every value, and structural deep equality; `toEndWith` retains only the check of suffix position.

Withdraw the existing contract for `toContainValues` if a direct call shows that the second argument is not an array of values to look for, or if any requested value is missing but the call still returns a pass. Withdraw the boundary description for `toEndWith` if the module explicitly treats containment in the middle as a suffix match. If any of these conditions occurs, keep the input and actual output and replace the relevant section on this page; do not sidestep the difference by continuing to use the broad term "containment."

Only two items remain to be filled in: the counting rules for duplicate requested values, and the actual result from `toEndWith` for an empty suffix. These do not prevent finalizing the all-members call semantics in this round, but they should not be treated as settled.

import predicate from './predicate';

# Troubleshooting Tree: String Normalization and Freezing

If a matcher related to 1.8 produces an unexpected result or message, first check whether the symptom concerns comparison, object state, or the failure message. Two symptoms can occur in the same run, but record their reviews separately.

```text
Unexpected result or message
├─ Inputs differ only in case
│  ├─ Save received and expected unchanged
│  ├─ Record the actual type before the call
│  ├─ Record pass from the directly returned object
│  └─ If there is no direct output, stop at the normalization check
├─ Object state does not match expectations
│  ├─ Record how the object was constructed
│  ├─ Record the call entry point and state result
│  ├─ Keep the full failure message
│  └─ Record the message call shape separately
└─ Both branches occur together
   ├─ Run standalone string inputs first
   ├─ Then run standalone object inputs
   └─ Do not attribute the combined output to a single file
```

## Earlier claims

The first version described case handling as "the entry point already converts everything to lowercase." That statement was later marked **obsolete**: it was a guess based on the call name, not a declaration directly visible in `src/matchers/toBeTrue/index.js`. For object-state failures, there was also a guess that `expected` in the message must have been appended by the wrapper layer. Without the full failure text, that claim can no longer be treated as a conclusion.

The old file is still worth opening as a starting point. From `jest-matcher-utils`, it imports `matcherHint`, `printExpected`, and `printReceived`, and it imports predicate functions from `./predicate`; local declarations include `predicate`, `passMessage`, `failMessage`, and `pass`. These names show that the file is an existing JavaScript matcher module; they do not establish that `toEqualCaseInsensitive` or `toBeFrozen` is implemented here.

## Review boundaries

For the string branch, retain at least the raw values, actual types, and direct return results. Terminal rendering may change colors, line breaks, or formatting; it cannot replace the returned object. A test name only tells you what it is meant to cover; it is not enough to establish the types of the values passed in.

In the object branch, treat state and the message as two separate observations. A correct state result does not mean the failure message's public shape is also correct; a plausible-looking message is no substitute for checking how the object was constructed. If all you have is a screenshot, first save the full text shown in it. Do not take just the last line as the complete message.

When opening the old file, start with the imports and local declarations. If you cannot find the target matcher's actual call or export relationship, go back and check the caller. Seeing `predicate` is not enough to link it directly to string normalization or object state.

## A failed attempt

An earlier plan was to change the test expectations first to turn the failure into a pass, then fill in the investigation record afterward. That approach has been abandoned because it would lose the original failure message and make it impossible to distinguish changes in the comparison result from changes in the message text. If a rerun is needed, first copy the inputs, object construction, and call entry point; without those originals, do not use modified expectations as a substitute for the original failure.

This page still has no saved direct-call output. If the string issue lacks the original values and direct results, stop at insufficient input evidence; if the object issue lacks the construction method, stop at the state branch; if the full message is missing, stop at the message-shape branch. Even if both branches occur, record them separately.

# String Normalization and Freezing Troubleshooting Tree

### First, triage by the observed symptoms

The call result is wrong, the object state is wrong, and the failure message looks wrong: these three descriptions often appear in the same troubleshooting record. Do not combine them into a single implementation issue at the outset. Save the evidence under the following branches:

```text
matcher issue
├─ Unexpected return result
│  ├─ Save the original received and expected values before the call
│  ├─ Save the actual types on both sides and the directly returned object
│  ├─ pass differs from expectations: keep the returned object and stop at the result branch
│  └─ Only terminal text is available: do not infer input types from the text
├─ Unexpected object state
│  ├─ Record how the object was constructed
│  ├─ Record the call entry point and state result
│  ├─ The state is reproducible: move on to the failure message
│  └─ Construction details are missing: stop at the state branch
├─ Unexpected failure message
│  ├─ Keep the original text from the first line to the last
│  ├─ Do not remove expect(...), arguments, or line breaks
│  ├─ The call shape is clear: record it separately from the state result
│  └─ Only the last line of a screenshot is available: stop at the message-shape branch
└─ All three occur together
   ├─ First, make a minimal string call
   ├─ Then, make a separate object call
   ├─ Keep the result and message for each call separately
   └─ Without independent original evidence, do not attribute them to a shared cause
```

If the issue only involves differences in input case, the first step is not to open a directory that looks related, but to save both inputs exactly as they are. For the object-state branch, save the construction details first; two values that both display as objects may have been constructed differently. Look at failure messages last to avoid revising earlier judgments based on the message.

### Entry-point record from 2023

When this record was first created, troubleshooting began with "Can we find a file that can be opened?" The old record pointed the issue name and call name to `src/matchers/toBeTrue/index.js`. The code visible at the top of the file at the time was:

```js
import { matcherHint, printExpected, printReceived } from 'jest-matcher-utils';
import predicate from './predicate';
```

The same area also contained `matcherHint`, `printExpected`, `printReceived`, `predicate`, `passMessage`, `failMessage`, and `pass`. The index described it as an existing JavaScript matcher module, suitable for reading the code and checking historical behavior.

This is as far as the entry-point assessment should go. It supports starting with the file header and local declarations, but not determining where the target matcher belongs from the path name. In particular, the filename `toBeTrue` does not justify putting string normalization, object state, and all Boolean checks into it.

### A previously used working rule

An early note said: "If the predicate passes, the call name can be used to determine case-handling behavior; look at object-state messages last." This original text is still retained, but is now marked **deprecated**. It linked the file, `predicate`, and the target matcher too hastily, and prioritized names over direct output.

There were two lines of inference at the time. First, having case-insensitive in the name might mean that case handling had already been completed before the call entered the matcher. Second, `expected` in the failure message might have been added by a common wrapper layer. Both only guided where to look first; neither was a conclusion drawn from call results. Without direct inputs, return values, and complete messages, they cannot be elevated to statements about behavior.

### On-call margin notes

Later margin notes narrowed the sequence to three steps: first record the original inputs or object construction, then record the direct result, and finally save the failure message. Types cannot be inferred from how values look when printed in the terminal. Nor can only the last line of a message be kept, because that line usually lacks the call shape.

The original evidence for the string branch includes `received`, `expected`, the types before the call, and the directly returned object. The original evidence for the object branch includes the construction method, call entry point, state result, and entire message. When both branches occur together, first split the compound call into two minimal calls; if independent inputs cannot be separated out, preserve the combined observations rather than recording a shared implementation point.

When opening `src/matchers/toBeTrue/index.js`, first inspect the import of `jest-matcher-utils`, then inspect `./predicate` and the local message and return-value declarations. If the file provides no new call or export relationships, return to the actual caller. Paths can help locate code, but cannot replace call relationships.

### Methods tried that failed to preserve the original evidence

There was once a plan to change the test expectations first, turning failures into passes, and then organize the record based on the new results. This method was later discontinued. Changing expectations overwrites the original failure, making it impossible afterward to tell whether the change came from the comparison result or the message text. Before rerunning, copy the inputs, object construction, and call entry point; without these, a passing result after modification cannot be used to backfill the earlier observations.

Another shortcut was to save only a final line like this:

```text
Expected: frozen object
Received: mutable object
```

This indicates that object state was involved, but does not show the matcher's call shape or whether the text was output directly by the module. It is now retained only as an old example in the appendix.

### Boundaries redrawn after review

A review explicitly separated "the result is correct" and "the message is correct" into two tracks. Comparison results require inputs, types, and the directly returned object; object state requires construction details and the state result; failure messages require the original text to be preserved separately. An unusual-looking message does not directly invalidate the state assessment, and a correct state result does not justify ignoring the call shape in the message.

The review also pointed out that the old file can serve only as a navigation aid for the local code. The import list and local declarations support inspecting `matcherHint`, `printExpected`, `printReceived`, `predicate`, `passMessage`, `failMessage`, and `pass`, but this page does not establish a direct relationship between `toEqualCaseInsensitive` and that file. # toStartWith Compatibility Review Workflow

This page preserves the migration path used when 1.8 was closed out. When people reference it, they often first jump to early single-module examples, then treat omissions on the registry side as intermittent loading issues; older records did in fact recommend this, so they have not been deleted. The review should now be done separately for the module, public entry point, and failure message.

Initially, `src/matchers/toBeTrue/index.test.js` was used as the reference because the two imports at the top of the file are straightforward: `jest-each` provides parameterized examples, and `./` points to the local `matcher`. This helps with reading the existing tests, but it never automatically connected `toStartWith` to the public matcher registry. The early draft wrote "the local matcher is called" as "the entry point is already available"; this part is outdated.

## Old Migration Order (Retained)

The old practice was to get the standalone module running first, then add the registry wiring in one pass at the end. The advantage was that local failures were easy to read; the problem was that a module example could still be green when an import was missing or the registry did not expose an entry of the same name. The recovery method at the time was also crude: whenever cumulative loading showed an issue, fall back to the single-module example and continue investigating. It helps narrow the failure surface, but it can hide the fact that the public entry point was not included in validation.

The old diagram remains here to make the checking gap at the time easier to identify:

```text
Single-module example ──passes──> Consider migration complete
       \
        └── registry wiring left until the end
```

## Later Revision

The review changed the migration to two independent checks. First verify how the module evaluates the input, then verify whether the public entry with the same name is imported, exposed, and can be loaded as part of the cumulative registry. The latter is not an incidental cleanup item; it determines whether users can obtain this matcher through the public registration mechanism.

toStartWith receives a string and a prefix and returns pass based on the actual prefix relationship; the public entry with the same name must also be imported correctly and exposed in the public matcher registry so that the cumulative registry remains loadable.

This sentence supersedes the early working judgment that the single-module example was sufficient, but it does not require retiring the old example. During migration, it is still possible to use the local example first to confirm the string and prefix, then switch to the registry path. The two checks target different things: the first concerns the matcher's return judgment, while the second concerns the public entry point and cumulative loading. Only when the latter shows a problem should the registry changes be reverted first; do not change the prefix judgment itself just to restore loading.

```text
Module: string + prefix ──> pass judgment
                         
Public entry: import ──> registry exposure ──> cumulative registry loading
```

## `toBeFrozen` Message Branch

Another line should not be inferred from the result of `toStartWith`. The issue with `toBeFrozen` is the failure-message shape: the object-state judgment and the message header visible to the caller are adjacent but distinct objects. Early records said "first reuse another matcher's template," but that did not hold up; if the sample result and the actual entry differ, confirm the message format for the current call with the person responsible for this item, core-05.

The failure-message shape for toBeFrozen still needs to be confirmed against the current call. Retain the complete input, version, and raw output, and cross-check them with the person responsible for this item, core-05; this page only provides a verification entry point, not a message template.

On this migration path, first preserve the normal call that triggers the failure, then read the raw diagnostics; afterward, compare only the message header. If registry loading and a message change appear at the same time, separate them in order: first restore the old registry wiring to obtain a loadable set, then restore the message path separately. Do not roll back both changes together and then declare that they had the same cause.

## Operation Sequence That Still Applies

1. From the local matcher example, confirm that `toStartWith` receives a string and a prefix.
2. Wire in the public entry with the same name and load it from the cumulative registry.
3. If loading fails, revert only the registry changes for that entry, while retaining the module-side check results.
4. Take another failing call for `toBeFrozen` and confirm that the diagnostic does not include the expected parameter.
5. If the message is wrong, restore the previous message-generation path; do not also adjust the object-state judgment.

This record does not assign the earlier `toBeTrue` test to the implementation of `toStartWith`; it only preserves the entry point used at the time to inspect the local matcher and parameterized example. If new examples are added later, place them at each matcher's own test location, rather than continuing to pile every registry regression into this page.

One old question remains unresolved: whether the failure text after loading the cumulative registry is identical character for character to that from the standalone entry. The call shape for `toBeFrozen` is fixed here, but no complete output that could substitute for the normal call has been saved, so this page remains suitable as a migration record, not as the sole source for message examples.

# Proposal for Negative-Number Messages and Even-Number Boundaries

The original draft grouped these two issues under "just add a check." That wording is retained here to explain why we later chose not to follow it directly. At the time, it was based only on the structure of a neighboring matcher's file: in `src/matchers/toBeTrue/index.js`, the imports from `jest-matcher-utils` are `matcherHint`, `printExpected`, and `printReceived`, followed by a local import of `predicate`; the file contains `passMessage`, `failMessage`, and the exported `pass`. That was enough to suggest changes at separate layers, but not enough to establish a particular message format or input range as the convention in use.

The review split the issues apart. The dispute over toBeNegative was not "can negative numbers be checked?" but what callers see on failure. The early proposal advocated reusing a generic message with expected, on the grounds that all numeric matchers could share a template. That reasoning did not hold up: an expected slot in a template does not mean the matcher actually has an expected parameter that callers can supply. Without a corresponding input, printing an apparently configurable expected would mislead debugging instead.

The failure-message format for toBeFrozen still needs to be checked against how it is called now. Keep the complete input, version, and raw output, and check with core-05, who owns this item; this page only provides a starting point for verification, not a message template.

For toBeNegative, there are still two candidate approaches:

- Make the failure message state only received, suitable for assertions with no additional comparison value;
- Keep the expected display, but only if the interface really passes a comparison value to the matcher and its meaning on failure can be explained.

The old draft defaulted to the second approach. Continuing with that default is not recommended at this stage. JXE-207 track an outstanding gap: recording only what is actually returned or thrown through the public entry point. Until that record is complete, the import of `printExpected` in a static file must not be treated as evidence that toBeNegative has to print expected. If the actual output differs from the candidate message, revert the message-template change, retain the predicate-side comparison work, and do not also standardize formatting in the same change.

The other half, toBeEven, is more straightforward, but it still cannot be reduced to "even just means integer." The trial needs to establish which inputs the matcher accepts, which inputs simply fail, and which need to be rejected before evaluation. The original proposal lumped nonnumeric inputs, non-integers, and zero into one bucket of counterexamples; that would leave callers unable to distinguish whether it was checking parity or type. Three categories remain to be observed: numeric inputs that fail the even-number condition, numeric boundary inputs, and nonnumeric inputs. They may not need three different messages, but we cannot assume in advance that they take the same branch.

JXE-224 require the relevant module maintainer to verify the even-number boundaries in the current version and provide an entry point for further inspection. Until that entry point is available, this proposal does not extend "even-number boundaries" into a guarantee covering all numeric objects. In particular, other matchers' use of `predicate` must not be taken to mean that the tool already covers boundary handling in toBeEven; what is needed here is this matcher's actual behavior, not similarity in neighboring filenames.

The trial changes can be implemented in this order: first retain one failure sample for each issue; then check the message against the hint's parameter structure to see whether it implies a nonexistent expected; finally, decide whether the predicate should handle type filtering only after the input classification for toBeEven is clear. Do not combine message samples and boundary samples into one "broad compatibility" test, or later failures will still leave it unclear whether the message has drifted or the scope of the check has changed.

The rollback conditions are also narrower than in the old draft. If the public result from toBeNegative has no expected slot, any change requiring an expected display should be reverted; if boundary inputs for toBeEven behave inconsistently through the existing entry point, first stop standardizing the messages, and do not use the hint layer to hide differences in the checks. Both issues can be reviewed in the same round, but they do not have to be completed in the same commit.

This record still retains the early advice to "just use the structure of toBeTrue as a reference," because people will return to it through old links. That advice can now only be used to find where to start reading the message functions and predicates. For exception paths involving module registration and object key sets, see DOC-17; those should not be pulled into the scope of this trial.

# Deep-Equality Predicate and Own-Keys Decision

1.8 This closeout effort did not initially start from a unified design. The records listed two names side by side: the deep-equality predicate of `toBeOneOf`, and all own keys of `toContainKeys`. Both have the appearance of set-membership checks, so at first glance it would be easy to write, "Find a common predicate, then adjust them together." The decision ultimately retained was exactly the opposite: first separate comparison of candidate values from the scope of object keys, and discuss a shared change only when reference material actually connects the two tracks.

The distinction behind this decision is not complex, but it affects the order of verification. `toBeOneOf` is concerned with the comparison relationship between received values and candidate items; `toContainKeys` is concerned with whether all keys owned by an object are present. A candidate item is a value used for comparison, while a key is a name obtained from an object. Calling both of them "set members" saves words, but hides the fact that their input shapes and failure results may differ. The draft therefore did not choose a "set predicate" as the shared implementation for the two requirements, nor did it casually interpret "deep equality" as some specific API.

## Early Entry

The earliest surviving location that could be opened was:

```js
// src/matchers/toBeTrue/predicate.test.js
import each from 'jest-each';
import predicate from './predicate';
```

The declaration that can be located in the file is `each(import, line 1)`. This fragment confirms only two narrow points: the test file references `jest-each` and imports `predicate` from a relative path; the repository index labels it an existing js module, suitable for code reading and checking historical behavior. It still cannot establish whether `toBeOneOf` calls the predicate here, much less whether `toContainKeys` obtains object keys from here.

The early investigation started from this file because the issue name and call name once led the reading to an actual test entry point. This route can be retained as navigation, but cannot be elevated into an ownership determination. The marker in the file path, `toBeTrue`, the imported `predicate`, and the parameterized test utility `jest-each` each support only their own local observation. They do not form a matcher registry, nor do they provide a reference chain between the two objects under review.

There was a relatively convenient candidate approach at the time: abstract both requirements into the same kind of "check whether several members satisfy a predicate," first change the shared check, and then have each matcher pass its own input. This approach was not adopted. Not because sharing a utility is necessarily wrong, but because there was no shared call relationship in hand, and the "members" on the two sides were not the same kind of thing. If the abstraction came first, it would later be difficult to determine from the result whether a difference came from comparing candidate values or from the scope of key retrieval; once the upstream input was still unconfirmed, the shared interface would also lock in an unconfirmed field shape.

## What Each Track Retained

### `toBeOneOf`

The name of this track is "Current-Version Result Differences in the Deep-Equality Predicate." It records the behavioral direction to verify, not a sample that has already been reproduced. The records contain no concrete received values, candidate list, failure output, or user call code, so an object, array, or primitive cannot be substituted for the missing case.

The local decision at the time was to treat deep equality as the comparison semantics under review, first confirm `toBeOneOf`'s own module, registry location, and test entry, and then determine whether it leads back to a predicate. This prevents "deep equality" from being misread as reference equality or textual equality, and also avoids inferring implementation ownership from the location of `predicate.test.js`.

This track was not written as a current-implementation conclusion that deep equality had already been adopted. The existing records support only the statement that the requirement history calls for checking the deep-equality predicate. If a later caller or test provides a concrete value shape, it will be possible to explain where the comparison occurs and what the compatibility difference looks like; until then, a shared public predicate is only a candidate approach, not a decision already made.

### `toContainKeys`

The constraint on the other track is "all own keys." "Own" cannot be omitted and replaced with an ordinary key set, because it changes the scope of the object that must be checked. The old records provide no object sample and do not state whether the prototype chain, non-enumerable properties, or symbol keys are included, so no particular enumeration function or complete boundary table can be filled in here.

The retained decision on this side is narrow: verification must consider both the source of the keys and the requirement that they be "all"; the result that any key matched cannot be used as a substitute. Nor can it be written as candidate-array matching merely because it entered the 1.8 closeout at the same time as `toBeOneOf`. One requirement focuses on value comparison, while the other focuses on the coverage of an object's own properties; similar names are not evidence of a shared implementation.

Directly reusing the predicate from the deep-equality side was considered here, converting key names into members to be compared first. This approach was set aside. It would hide the own-object scope restriction inside the conversion step and could not answer the missing-caller question. Based on the existing material, finding the actual adopter, entry point, and result is more reliable than first designing an adapter layer that turns keys into values.

## Boundaries After Review

The subsequent review did not turn the early entry into a shared implementation. The reading order to retain is: first inspect the module and registry for the matcher under review, then check back whether it references `predicate`; if handling `toContainKeys`, separately confirm the scope from which the keys are obtained. The existence of the test file only shows that this adjacent path is worth opening; it cannot replace a call relationship.

This distinction also explains why "start by looking from the predicate" in the draft caused a misreading. As a workflow, it means starting with the tests in the file already found; as an implementation conclusion, it is too broad. The latter interpretation should be withdrawn. Likewise, "both requirements can be covered by one set check" is only a convenient phrase from the early discussion, not the rationale for the 1.8 change.

If a first landing point must be chosen between the two options, the record favors retaining two independent review tracks rather than establishing a shared change:

- First confirm `toBeOneOf`'s candidate input and comparison call, then discuss whether the deep-equality predicate needs adjustment.
- First confirm the adopter of `toContainKeys` and the source of its object keys, then discuss the boundaries of "all own keys" in the implementation.
- Before evidence for both items appears, do not treat the test-file path, the `jest-each` import, or the relative `predicate` import as proof of matcher ownership.

These three points were the actual work scope decided at the time. They did not promise that the two matchers would never share a lower-level utility; they only constrained the way to infer things before making a change. If a clear reference chain appears later, the shared relationship can be recorded in the implementation materials; the early requirement's meaning cannot be rewritten retroactively merely because the two may share something.

## Changes After the Card Notes

JXE-211 moved from To Do to Blocked in the historical actions of 2025-10-10, with the reason that the upstream interface owner had not yet confirmed the input fields. This note makes the stopping point on the `toBeOneOf` side clearer: before the input fields are confirmed, it is not possible to reliably determine the value received by the matcher, where the candidate items come from, or use a new abstraction to bypass this gap. Blocking did not negate the requirement name "deep-equality predicate"; it only prevented it from being expanded into a complete implementation conclusion.

Therefore, the original candidate approach of "build the shared predicate first" should be regarded as withdrawn on this track. The shared predicate can neither confirm the upstream fields nor conjure a user path out of nowhere; if code were written first, the unconfirmed input would be masked by an internal interface name. The retained action is to wait for material about the input fields while continuing to keep the behavior name and the known test entry separate.

JXE-228 left a verification requirement on the `toContainKeys` side: find a caller that is still using this matcher and check the actual version, entry point, and current result. The card does not provide evidence that a caller has already been found, so here we do not state "still in use" as a verified fact. It only indicates where the gap is: this track needs an adopter sample, not another abstract set definition.

The roles of the two cards cannot be interchanged. JXE-211 stop the deep-equality track at the input fields; JXE-228 stop the own-key track at checking the caller, version, and result. The former cannot prove that the latter has no caller, and the latter cannot determine the former's input shape. In this history, they appear only as entry points for subsequent verification.

DOC-21 is an adjacent interface review record. It and this page both concern matcher compatibility, but this page does not rewrite the other page's failure wording or discussion of a custom every set as an implementation decision for "all own keys." What is retained here is how the requirements were split, which approaches were set aside, and where each track is blocked.

## Retaining and Withdrawing the Old Wording

The old records contain a passage saying that both objects could first be classified as "set members satisfy predicate." This passage is still worth retaining in the history because it explains why the early investigation placed the two requirements side by side; however, it is no longer an actionable check. It neither distinguishes candidate values from object keys nor shows that the input fields and the caller have yet to be confirmed independently. If later readers extract only this sentence, they may easily think that finding a shared predicate completes the compatibility closeout.

Also retained, but with a narrower use, is the suggestion to start reading from `src/matchers/toBeTrue/predicate.test.js`. It can still lead to the direct imports `each` and `./predicate`, making it suitable for reviewing local test style. It cannot answer whether `toBeOneOf` calls deep equality through that predicate, nor whether `toContainKeys` checks only own keys. The path is adjacent navigation, not a mapping from requirements to implementation.

In this draft, the decision that remains valid can be compressed into one sentence: first verify the two compatibility tracks independently, and do not adopt a shared abstraction until there is direct material for each one's input, caller, and behavioral result. This is a work boundary in the history, not a complete account of later behavior.

## Decision State Diagram

This diagram shows when the two investigation tracks may discuss a shared abstraction; it does not represent the matcher's internal implementation. When input or adopter material is missing, return to the respective verification entry point.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Split20: Value-comparison and own-key tracks recorded
    Split20 --> ValueReady20: Candidate input and comparison result complete
    Split20 --> KeysReady20: Adopter and key source complete
    ValueReady20 --> JointReview20: Reference relationship verifiable
    KeysReady20 --> JointReview20: Boundary sample can be rerun
    JointReview20 --> KeepSplit20: No evidence of a shared call
    JointReview20 --> Shared20: Direct evidence of shared dependency
```

# Key Failure Messages and Collection Approaches

This proposal starts with two very small interface surfaces: one named call requires an explanation of whether a key exists, while the other preserves the collection result of a custom every. Both look like failure-message wording issues, but in practice they are not necessarily determined by the same piece of code. Keep this distinction for now to avoid changing the checks, registration, and callers all at once just to unify the wording.

The initial draft only listed candidate approaches and treated `src/matchers/toBeTrue/index.js` as a possible shared entry point. After reviewing this file, what can be confirmed is still limited: the file header contains

```js
import { matcherHint, printExpected, printReceived } from 'jest-matcher-utils';
import predicate from './predicate';
```

The visible declarations include `matcherHint`, `printExpected`, `printReceived`, `predicate`, `passMessage`, `failMessage`, and `pass`; `predicate` is on line 3, and `pass` is on line 21. The repository index describes its local role as an existing js module for reading code and checking historical behavior. This can provide leads for tracing message assembly and check entry points, but it is not enough to attribute the implementation of `toContainKey` or `toContainKeys` to this file. The proposal therefore retains the path as a starting point for verification, rather than describing it as a confirmed shared implementation.

## Three Approaches from the Initial Draft

The first approach is for the two matchers to maintain their failure messages separately. `toContainKey` can structure its message around the received object, the key being checked, and the keys actually found; `toContainKeys` can retain the context of the collection check, explaining that a member failed the custom every rather than presenting the whole collection generically as a single deep equality comparison. The advantages are localized changes and a clear rollback path, while the drawback is that similar combinations of `matcherHint`, expected, and received may gradually diverge.

The second approach is to extract a shared message-building function. It could accept the matcher name, the expected value, and received, with the caller adding local details about own keys or collection members. This would make it easier to keep formatting consistent, but would also lock in compatibility relationships that have not yet been confirmed. If the two matchers have different failure conditions, the shared function may end up merely putting two sets of rules back into its parameters; there is currently no evidence to justify that coupling just because the wording is similar.

The third approach is to leave the shared structure untouched for now and only add records of fixed inputs and outputs at the two boundaries. First identify the actual registration relationships for the existing entry points, then save failure samples separately. This approach cannot automatically resolve duplicated formatting, but it can answer more practical questions: whether callers are actually seeing a missing own key on an object or a failed custom check within a collection; whether the current version already has consumers that depend on some legacy wording. The reviewed version still treats this as the first experimental approach, with the second approach retained only as a later option.

## Local Scope to Try First

The first set of samples for `toContainKey` should distinguish two objects: one where the key is on the object itself, and one where the key is only on the prototype chain. The same "exists" conclusion cannot be used for both. Failure samples must at least show received and the target key, so callers do not get just a sentence with no object context. The initial discussion here is about what the message should contain, without first specifying new public fields or changing the exported name of the matcher.

Samples for `toContainKeys` should be split by collection behavior. When all members of a collection pass, record the normal result; when a member is judged to have failed by the custom every, record the failure position or identifiable member context; keep an empty collection as a separate case, because it may reveal confusion between "no objects to check" and "no failures after checking". If the existing interface returns only a boolean result, the proposal does not require changing the return shape to display a position, and the first step is to confirm whether the failure message can fill in the information without breaking callers.

The custom every must not be silently replaced with a standard deep equality comparison. A standard comparison is suitable for showing whether an expected value equals received, but cannot show that every member of the collection has gone through the check specified by the caller. Conversely, the need to display a failing member must not lead to exposing all the internal checking details for every member in the public message. The experiment retains only the minimum context that helps locate the difference; overly detailed expansion of internal objects would make both old snapshots and the reading experience unstable.

The shared portions of failure messages should continue to reuse this project's existing message utilities. `matcherHint`, `printExpected`, and `printReceived` are already explicit local dependencies in the currently visible file, so the experiment should first compare their ordering and inputs rather than invent another string format. Here, "reuse" only means continuing to trace back through the existing code, and which file or wrapper layer the target matchers actually call has not yet been confirmed. If no corresponding call can be found, leave the item blank rather than filling it in with the name of a neighboring file.

## Material Added after the Review

[JXE-212] later recorded a `caller_walkthrough` action. The available material only indicates that a caller walkthrough was performed and gives no caller version, entry path, or actual result, so it supports the conclusion that "verification is needed at the point of use", but not a claim that a specific version already depends on a particular piece of wording. The corresponding card still requires finding a caller that still uses the name in question and checking its version, entry point, and current result, and these three items remain open on this page.

The description in [JXE-229] retains the observation that legacy calls use custom every results from `toContainKeys`, and requires checks following the repository maintainers' routine steps. Here, "legacy calls" only means that the card contains this historical lead, and does not establish that all callers use the same collection shape. The proposed experiment should first find a reproducible call, then determine whether samples need to be added for other collection forms.

These two pieces of material change the priorities of the initial draft. The initial draft was primarily concerned with whether the two matcher messages needed to be unified; now it is more important to first confirm exactly which part of the result the legacy calls depend on. If callers only check the boolean value, the compatibility risk of wording changes may be lower; if callers paste failure output into regression materials, the wording and the ordering of expected/received need more care. The current material does not give the actual breakdown of these two cases, so no particular risk can be declared to have disappeared in advance.

## Trade-offs in the Review

The main cost of keeping the wording local is that the two implementations may continue to produce similar but not identical messages. This cost can be detected through fixed samples rather than hidden behind a shared function from the outset. The main cost of a shared function is that it becomes a new dependency boundary, and any special semantics of either matcher must be expressed through parameters; until the relationship between the targets has been verified, this boundary is harder to roll back than duplicated wording.

Another trade-off is whether to include "own key" in public failure messages. For `toContainKey`, this is one of the most useful distinctions for callers interpreting results, but if the current version already has stable legacy wording, adding the term directly may cause snapshot changes. The proposal recommends first putting own keys and prototype-chain keys into the experimental samples, comparing the actual readability gains, and then deciding whether the term belongs in the full message or should remain only in the test output. Without existing output samples, no particular layout should be presented as a compatibility requirement.

Collection every has a similar issue. Showing the first failing member makes it easier to locate the problem, but the custom check may depend on member order, and when multiple members fail, showing only one may lead readers to think there is only one problem. Showing all failing members, on the other hand, may expand large objects into unstable text. The first version of the experiment only needs to distinguish "collection check failure" from "single-value deep equality failure", with the decision on whether to list multiple members left until real output is available.

The reason for not choosing a one-shot rewrite is also stated here: the only clearly identified source-code location at present is in the `toBeTrue` file, and it exposes several declarations covering message utilities, predicates, and matcher routines. It can help explain common organizational patterns in this repository, but cannot fill in the missing exports, callers, or registry relationships for the target objects. Expanding the write-up based directly on the filename would mistake navigation clues for implementation evidence and would also make the rollback scope unclear.

## What the Experiment Records Should Contain

Each sample should record the call name, the basic shape of received, the target key or collection, the checking method used, and the final failure text displayed. Record object own keys and prototype-chain keys separately; also record the cases where all members of a collection pass, one member fails, and the collection is empty separately. The records do not need to copy the entire object, only enough to show why the two inputs produce different results. If an input cannot be reproduced through the current entry point, record only the entry point and the missing items, without substituting a guessed sample.

Code changes should initially stay close to messages and local tests, without simultaneously changing the matcher registry, export relationships, or unrelated matchers. This keeps two types of changes separate: the readability of failure messages, and whether the custom every in `toContainKeys` still aggregates results in the same way as the legacy calls. If verification finds that the target implementation is not at the existing path, first update the trace-back entry point, then decide whether the changes need to be moved; do not treat a neighboring module as a substitute for confirming where the implementation actually belongs.

The observed results should answer at least three questions. First, whether `toContainKey` lets readers distinguish a missing own key from a key that exists only on the prototype chain. Second, whether `toContainKeys`, when custom every fails, still lets readers know that the failure occurred in a collection check rather than interpreting it as an ordinary single-value comparison. Third, whether legacy callers depend only on pass or fail, or also on some stable fragment of the message. These three results are not currently available, so they are exit criteria for the experiment, not statements that acceptance has already been completed.

## Open Items and Rollback Criteria

Three specific confirmations are still missing: the actual version and entry point of a caller using `toContainKey`; one real collection sample using the custom every in `toContainKeys`; which implementation layer each of the two calls points to in the current registry. The walkthrough action in JXE-212 cannot substitute for these results, and the description in JXE-229 cannot prove that other callers use the same form. If this material cannot be obtained, the proposal will remain a set of candidate approaches, without presenting local guesses as public behavior.

If the local experiment only changes message formatting without improving the distinction between own keys and collection checks, roll back the message changes and retain the trace-back records. If the shared builder function needs to accept a large number of matcher-specific cases, roll back the extraction approach and return to separate wording. If real callers depend on the old wording, retain it for now and add diagnostic samples that do not affect existing results, without migrating the callers in the same change.

Whether to ultimately adopt a shared builder function depends on whether the two implementations found really share the same message boundary; whether to include own keys and failing members in public messages depends on the existing output and how callers use it. The current version can proceed to local review, but neither of these choices can be marked as decided yet. The relevant code entry point is still `src/matchers/toBeTrue/index.js`, and the repository is `internal/jest-extended`'s `v_prev`; continue verification from here by following declarations and calls before making any actual changes.
